newsitem.title: UK: EMU tangle leaves bond investors seeking strategy.
newsitem.headline: EMU tangle leaves bond investors seeking strategy.

text.p: The latest chapter in the single currency saga has left European bond analysts dazed and confused, with theories on the fate of EMU ranging from a stronger euro to complete collapse.
They are counting on the Amsterdam summit next week to shed some light on the situation, but in the meantime, the one bit of common advise amid the confusion is stay away until the dust settles.
"The safest thing investors can do is look to avoid these markets altogether over this time period," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW here.

France's new left-wing government caused another EMU kerfuffle on Monday when it said it wanted time to review the stability pact -- a system of censures and fines intended to ensure fiscal discipline after monetary union.
The pact, agreed after hard-fought negotiations in Dublin in December, is due to be ratified by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam next Monday and Tuesday.
Investors determined to try and cash in on the confusion should look to the short end of peripheral Europe, in particular Italy and Spain, said Reed.
"A trading recommendation that can perform under any scenario...is the front end of Italy and Spain which is where all the convergence potential is now," she said.

With two-year Spanish paper yielding around 170 basis points above its German counterpart, that gap would have to close significantly should European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) go ahead with Spain in the first wave.
And if it does not, possible rate cuts in Spain and likely curve steepening also make it a sensible place to be.
Some analysts were optimistic the set-back over the stability pact would be resolved without too much fall-out for bond markets.
"The French do want EMU -- just maybe a slightly different type of EMU from the Germans," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International.
"They will see how far they can push it, but they won't push it over the edge."
Brickman said most of the bad news on EMU had already been priced in to the market.
"Perhaps there's a bit more downside, but unless there's a wide rift between the French and Germans, we're unlikely to see significant slippage from current levels."
He said any such slide should be seen as a buying opportunity ahead of expected agreement on the stability pact.

"Once we get agreement between Germany and France, then it will start to look like the political will is back, perhaps even stronger than before if they've come through this quite severe test," he said.
But David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London, was much more pessimistic and predicted a big shake-out in European bonds once the confusion clears.

"Europe is in crisis here and I don't think markets have fully taken account of that," he said. "They could hit the wall over the next few days as we run into the Franco-German summit on Friday and Amsterdam next week."
He said the reaction in Italy on Monday, when September BTP futures fell over a point, was just the start.
"The Italian rally is on the line here -- they've been the torch-bearers of convergence."
Brown predicted the Italian/German 10-year spread could widen as far as 275 basis points from its current 154 basis points.

On the other side of the coin, 10-year German Bund yields could fall as far as 5.25 percent this year, as their safe-haven status attracts nervous investors, said Brown. By 1015 GMT, 10-year yields were at 5.79 percent.
